intervention_label: TCR-T against next-generation hematopoietic minor-H antigens (UTA2-1 and other A*02:01-restricted mHAgs beyond HA-1/HA-2)
mechanism: UTA2-1 is an HLA-A*02:01-restricted peptide from the biallelic, hematopoiesis-restricted gene C12orf35; a donor T cell that recognizes the recipient's allelic version can kill blood-lineage cells, including leukemia, while sparing the epithelial tissues that drive GVHD. It broadens the mismatch pool beyond HA-1 and HA-2 to pairs that happen to differ at this locus.
rationale: This patient's primary handle is HLA-restricted GVL, but the clinical TCR-T products (TSC-100/101, Bleakley) only cover HA-1 and HA-2, and eligibility hangs on the pair carrying that specific disparity. UTA2-1 and the wider set of A*02:01 hematopoietic mHAgs give a fallback antigen if the HA-1/HA-2 genotyping comes back uninformative, keeping the GVL-without-GVHD route open. It is still gated on A*02:01 and on the patient/sibling differing at the antigen.
novelty: UTA2-1 sits at the antigen-discovery and patient-CTL-clone stage with no engineered TCR-T product or registered trial, unlike the HA-1/HA-2/WT1/PRAME programs that trial_screener already carries.

key_manuscripts.finding: Identified UTA2-1 as an HLA-A*02:01-restricted, hematopoiesis-restricted minor-H antigen from a myeloma patient in durable remission after DLI; UTA2-1-specific CTL lysed hematopoietic and malignant cells but left non-hematopoietic cells alone.

model_systems: hematopoietic vs non-hematopoietic cell cytotoxicity panels
developability: No clinical-grade TCR against UTA2-1 exists; a receptor would have to be isolated, validated, and built into a product before any trial. The delivery platform (donor-derived TCR-T on the back of an allo-HCT) is the same one already being used for HA-1/HA-2, so the path is at least charted.
risks: Needs the specific recipient-positive / donor-negative UTA2-1 disparity, which may not be present in this sibling pair any more than the HA-1/HA-2 one is.
On-target reach is limited to hematopoietic reconstitution, but antigen-loss escape remains possible given this patient's clonal evolution.
caveats: An antigen-discovery finding, not a therapeutic product; it widens the mHAg menu rather than offering something ready to give.

intervention_label: Next-generation TP53 Y220C stabilizer chemotypes (covalent tyrosine-mimic fragments; novel covalent scaffolds)
mechanism: The Y220C substitution opens a surface crevice that destabilizes the p53 DNA-binding domain; these compounds dock into that crevice, several of them forming a covalent bond to Cys220, and raise the mutant's melting temperature so it holds a wild-type-like fold. The covalent tyrosine-mimic fragments literally replace the aromatic ring lost in the mutation.
rationale: If TP53 is confirmed as Y220C, rezatapopt is the clinical option, but it is a single molecule from one sponsor and its myeloid single-agent activity is blunted by MDM2/XPO1/BCL-2 feedback. A structurally distinct, covalent backup chemotype would matter if rezatapopt fails, is inaccessible, or needs a longer-residence binder. These stay entirely contingent on first confirming the aberration and then confirming it is Y220C.
novelty: Distinct tool-compound chemotypes with no IND or trial; rezatapopt is the only Y220C molecule in clinical development and PhiKan083 is the tool compound already logged by researcher, so these are a separate, earlier branch.

key_manuscripts.finding: Screened SNAr electrophiles as covalent tyrosine mimics for Y220C; fragment SN001 raised the mutant melting temperature by ~4.5 C, bound Cys220 in the crevice by X-ray, and kept DNA-binding intact, offered as a starting point for optimization.
Used structure-based virtual screening and molecular dynamics to find C8, an indole-core covalent stabilizer whose enantiomers bond Cys124 and Cys220 and stabilize the Y220C fold in vitro.

developability: Fragments and virtual-screen hits, not lead compounds; cellular potency, apoptosis, PK and a myeloid model would all have to come before any human dosing. Years behind rezatapopt.
risks: No cellular kill or apoptosis shown; the Carter AML data predict Y220C reactivation alone is weakly pro-apoptotic and needs a venetoclax or MDM2/XPO1 partner.
Doubly gated: confirm the TP53 aberration, then confirm Y220C; a non-Y220C lesion makes the whole chemotype irrelevant.
Likely superseded by rezatapopt if that program succeeds in myeloid disease.
caveats: Same feedback-limited single-agent behavior as rezatapopt is expected, so any real use would be combination, not monotherapy.

intervention_label: Mutant-p53 destabilization via DNAJA1/HSP40 inhibition or statin repurposing
mechanism: DNAJA1, an HSP40 co-chaperone, binds misfolded conformational mutant p53 and shields it from CHIP-mediated degradation; blocking DNAJA1 (or lowering mevalonate output with a statin, which impairs the DNAJA1 interaction) shunts the mutant protein to the proteasome. Y220C is a thermolabile, misfolding mutant, so it is a plausible DNAJA1 client.
rationale: This is the opposite bet to reactivation: instead of refolding Y220C, degrade it. It is worth flagging because statins are cheap, available, and already taken by many patients, so a repurposing signal is easy to test, and it does not depend on the reactivator pharmacology. For this patient it is a hedge, not a plan, and the case for it in myeloid Y220C is thin.
novelty: A repurposing/synthetic-lethal hypothesis (statins, DNAJA1 tool compounds) with no oncology development program in AML and no trial; nothing upstream touches the destabilization axis.

key_manuscripts.finding: Showed DNAJA1 stabilizes misfolded conformational mutant p53 through the mevalonate pathway and that statins trigger CHIP-mediated degradation of the mutant, sparing wild-type and DNA-contact mutants.

model_systems: solid-tumor cell lines with conformational TP53 mutants
developability: Statins are approved and could be tested as a repurposing signal, but there is no AML program, no myeloid dose-response, and DNAJA1 inhibitors are only tool compounds. Everything published is in solid-tumor conformational mutants, not AML Y220C.
risks: Counter-productive mechanism concern: degrading mutant p53 removes any gain-of-function but does not restore tumor-suppressor activity, so it may do little on its own in a p53-null-behaving clone.
Whether AML Y220C behaves as a DNAJA1 client and responds to statin-driven degradation is untested.
Statin single-agent antileukemic effect is unproven; this is a mechanism to probe, not to prescribe.
caveats: Philosophically at odds with the rezatapopt reactivation route; the two should not be assumed to combine.

intervention_label: Epitope-edited donor HSPC graft enabling CD123/CD33-directed therapy without hematopoietic toxicity
mechanism: Single-base editing changes a few residues in the CD123 (or CD33/FLT3/KIT) epitope on donor stem cells so antibodies and CAR-T no longer recognize the healthy graft, while ligand binding and protein function are preserved. The engrafted, edited hematopoiesis becomes invisible to the targeting agent, so CD123/CD33 therapy can be pushed against leukemia without wiping out normal marrow.
rationale: This patient is CD123+ and CD33+ with documented clonal evolution, and a second allo-HCT is already on the table, so the graft is a thing that could, in principle, be engineered. Editing the donor graft would let a CD123- or CD33-directed agent run harder against escape-prone blasts after HCT2 without the myelotoxicity that normally caps those drugs. It lines up unusually well with the planned transplant platform.
novelty: A preclinical donor-graft-engineering concept with no clinical trial; it is a different idea from the CD123-CD33 cCAR and CLL-1/CD33/CD123 CAR-T products already surfaced, which target antigen directly rather than protecting normal marrow.

key_manuscripts.finding: Base-edited epitopes on donor HSPCs (including CD123 and CD33/FLT3/KIT) let the reconstituted hematopoiesis resist CAR-T and antibodies while staying functional, widening the therapeutic window for AML-directed immunotherapy in mouse models.

developability: Requires manufacturing an edited donor graft on top of an already complex second transplant, plus the regulatory package for a base-edited cell product. Real preclinical proof-of-concept exists, but nothing is enrolling and the lift is large.
risks: Layers base-editing genotoxicity and off-target unknowns onto a high-risk HCT2.
Adds substantial manufacturing and time cost when this patient has ~85% marrow blasts and needs cytoreduction now.
Benefit depends on then delivering a CD123/CD33 agent hard enough to matter, which reintroduces that agent's own toxicities.
caveats: Conceptually the neatest fit with the planned HCT2, but it is nowhere near clinical readiness and would not help the immediate disease burden.

intervention_label: Reversing post-transplant MHC class II downregulation to restore graft-versus-leukemia
mechanism: After allo-HCT, relapsing AML blasts often silence HLA class II epigenetically rather than mutating, which hides them from donor CD4 T cells; the loss is reversible, and interferon-gamma or hypomethylating agents can switch MHC-II back on. Restoring antigen presentation would re-expose the blasts to donor T cells and to any HLA-restricted TCR-T given as consolidation.
rationale: This is a textbook late GVL-escape relapse: CR for ~6 years after a matched-sibling transplant, then breakthrough, and this patient's own flow already notes HLA-DR variably decreased. If the escape is epigenetic MHC-II silencing rather than genetic HLA loss, an IFN-gamma or HMA priming step could make DLI, a second transplant, or WT1/HA-directed TCR-T actually bite. It is an adjunct to the cellular strategies, not a standalone therapy.
novelty: The escape biology is well described, but re-inducing MHC-II specifically to potentiate GVL or TCR-T has not been run as a registered strategy; it is a mechanism-to-therapy hypothesis distinct from the TCR-T products themselves.

key_manuscripts.finding: Post-HCT AML relapse was driven by an immune signature including epigenetic downregulation of HLA class II, which was reversible in culture with interferon-gamma rather than caused by new mutations.
Relapsed AML after allo-HCT showed downregulation of MHC class II genes as a recurrent immune-escape route, again reversible with interferon-gamma, pointing at a druggable epigenetic mechanism.
Described the competing genetic escape route, loss of the mismatched HLA haplotype via uniparental disomy of 6p, which is irreversible and would not respond to antigen-presentation priming.

model_systems: patient relapse vs diagnosis paired samples
interferon-gamma re-induction of MHC-II ex vivo
developability: The priming agents (IFN-gamma, azacitidine/decitabine) are available, so a re-induction step could be tested relatively quickly, but the escape mechanism in this specific patient has not been characterized and no protocol packages this as a GVL-restoration strategy.
risks: Re-inducing HLA class II and inflaming the graft could aggravate GVHD.
If the escape is genetic HLA loss rather than epigenetic silencing, priming does nothing and a donor change or non-HLA-restricted approach is needed instead.
Adjunctive only; it potentiates the cellular therapies rather than reducing the current 85% blast burden.
caveats: Whether this patient's relapse is epigenetic MHC-II silencing or genetic HLA loss is unknown and would determine whether the strategy is even relevant.

intervention_label: CD123-directed NK-cell engagers (SAR443579/IPH6101 NKp46xCD16 ANKET; AFM28 CD123xCD16A)
mechanism: Multispecific NK-cell engagers cross-link CD123 on blasts to NKp46 and CD16a on NK cells, redirecting innate cytotoxicity against CD123-high leukemic stem and progenitor cells, including CD123-low or CD64+ populations that resist plain ADCC.
rationale: On-mechanism for the patient's CD123 handle and framed as an LSC / antigen-escape hedge, which is why it was scanned.
exclusion_reason: Already clinical-stage, so this is trial_screener's territory, not the preclinical horizon: SAR443579/IPH6101 is in a Phase 1/2 first-in-human study (NCT05086315) in R/R AML/MDS with reported complete remissions, and AFM28 has likewise entered Phase 1. Both are past the earlier-than-clinical bar this file is bounded to.

intervention_label: MECOM (EVI1)-directed strategies for the relapse cytogenetic gain
mechanism: MECOM/EVI1 is an oncogenic transcription factor amplified/gained at this patient's relapse; proposed approaches (BET, LSD1, or CDK inhibition; transcriptional-dependency targeting) act on the programs it drives rather than the factor itself, which is largely undrugged.
rationale: Flagged in the horizon-scan brief because MECOM gain is an adverse relapse lesion, so it was worth checking whether any mechanism maps onto a stated feature.
exclusion_reason: MECOM/EVI1 is not among the patient's stated targetable_features, and no MECOM-directed mechanism plausibly maps onto CD123, CD33, TP53 Y220C, the HLA-restricted handles, or the transplant platform. Per the feature-scope rule it stays out; the targets field is a nominal placeholder only, not a real CD123 mechanism. EVI1 also remains an undrugged transcription factor with no candidate molecule to log.
